OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $F(N)$ be the size of the largest subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ which does not contain any set of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$. What is\[ \lim_{N\to \infty}\frac{F(N)}{N}?\]Is this limit irrational?
#168: [ErGr79][ErGr80]
additive combinatorics
This limit was proved to exist by Graham, Spencer, and Witsenhausen [GSW77], who showed it is equal to\[\frac{1}{3}\sum_{k\in K}\frac{1}{d_k},\]where $d_1<d_2<\cdots $are the $3$-smooth numbers and $K$ is the set of $k$ for which $f(k)>f(k-1)$, where $f$ counts the largest subset of $\{d_1,\ldots,d_k\}$ that avoids $\{n,2n,3n\}$.
Similar questions can be asked for the density or upper density of infinite sets without such configurations.
The limit can be estimated by elementary arguments (see the comments). Eberhard has used the formula of [GSW77] mentioned above to calculate the value of the limit as\[0.800965\cdots.\]
Additional thanks to: Sarosh Adenwalla, Boris Alexeev, Stijn Cambie, Jonathan Chapman, and Sean Eberhard

 The formula in [GrSpWi77] mentioned by Terry is very natural and one can fairly easily discover it for oneself. It starts with the observation that the problem naturally splits into a large number of disjoint subproblems, one for each number $x \le N$ divisible by neither $2$ nor $3$. It is also extremely practical for making rigorous estimates for the limit density (in particular, the limit density is computable). It reduces to doing some integer programming to find the values of $f(k)$. Using this approach I found that the limit density is $0.8009655909371?$ (where $?$ indicates that only the last digit is uncertain).

 The following elementary bounds can be proven easily:
$$\frac 45 \le \lim_{ N \to \infty} \frac{F(n)}{N} \le \frac 56$$
Take the complement of the integers in 
$$C=\cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]$$
then every set of the form $\{n,2n,3n\}$ where $1\le n \le \frac N3$ has exactly one element in $C$, since $2N/6^i<n<3n \le N/6^{i-1}$ is impossible (which would be the only way to avoid the elements in $C$).
In the other direction, as an improvement on the upper bound;
the sets $\{n,2n,3n\}$ for n in $B=\cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]  \setminus \left( \cup_{i=1}^{\infty} ]N/6^i, 4N/(3*6^i)] \cap 2\mathbb Z \right)$ are disjoint.
If two sets intersect, $\{n,2n,3n\} \cap \{n',2n',3n'\} \not= \emptyset$ for $n,n' \in B$, then $n,n' \in ]N/6^i, 2N/6^i]$ for some $i$ and $3n=2n'$, so $n$ is even and bounded by $2/3*2N/6^i.$
So this could not happen, so we had approximately $N/6$ disjoint triples.

 To add some amusing color: the conjecture "$f(k)=g(k)$ for all $k$" is false, with the first counterexample being $k=45$. Confusingly, they say they computed $f(k)$ for $k\le 50$; unfortunately, "Table 2" only includes the values for $k\le 25$.
The function $g(k)$ is very simple to compute (much simpler than $f(k)$), doable even by hand or in like a Google spreadsheet. I claim that $g(45)=15$ ("perfectly balanced" between the three classes). Meanwhile, $f(45)=14$, which can be checked at https://oeis.org/A094708 or by manually subtracting computing from https://oeis.org/A057561 .
There is definitely room for someone to write a modern version of the paper with much tighter bounds on $\lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{F(n)}{N}$ given the improvements in computational power. But I don't personally see it determining the value in any concrete sense, nor determining whether it is rational.

 In [GrSpWi77] the limit is shown to equal $\frac{1}{3} \sum_{k \in K} \frac{1}{d_k}$, where $d_1 < d_2 <\dots$ are the $3$-smooth numbers, $K$ is the set of $k$ for which $f(k) > f(k-1)$ (OEIS A004059), and $f(k)$ is the largest subset of $\{d_1,\dots,d_k\}$ that avoids $n,2n,3n$ (OEIS A057561). The authors speculate that $f(k) = 1 + \lfloor 2k/3 \rfloor$ if $k \neq 0 \hbox{ mod } 3$, and that an extremizer for $f(k)$ can always be chosen to be in a coset of $\langle 2^3, 2 \times 3 \rangle$ (this could be a typo, it seems more reasonable to conjecture that the extremizer *avoids* such a coset).
